content.title: Denver robbery triggers citywide emergency alert by mistake
content.text: To be compensated, Stephen Martinez would have to establish "actual innocence" in the 1998 death of a 4-month-old. DENVER — Stephen Martinez – freed from prison after a judge on Tuesday vacated his murder conviction in the 1998 death of a 4-month-old girl – could be eligible for nearly $2 million in compensation for the 27-plus years he spent behind bars. But there’s a hurdle he has to cross before being eligible for the money provided under a state law passed in 2013 aimed at redressing wrongful convictions: He has to convince a judge or jury that he’s actually innocent. “Our exoneration statute provides for no compensation if it was merely a situation where the evidence was not sufficient to prove an individual guilty beyond a reasonable doubt,” said Scott Robinson, a longtime defense attorney and 9NEWS legal analyst. In cases where a previously incarcerated person can show actual innocence, the law requires payment of $70,000 for each year behind bars. In Martinez’s case, that ads up to about $1.9 million. According to court documents obtained by 9NEWS Investigates, Martinez was watching Heather Mares – his girlfriend’s infant daughter – on Oct. 17, 1998, when he called 911 and reported she was choking. Responding police officers found bloody sheets in a washing machine, and doctors diagnosed her with a skull fracture. During police questioning, Martinez said he shook the crying baby and banged her head against a crib – and prosecutors asserted that he was guilty of what was then known as shaken baby syndrome. Attorneys for the Korey Wise Innocence Project took up his case and brought in outside experts to look at records in the case. Those experts concluded that Heather Mares died of a respiratory infection, not abuse, that the skull fracture could have occurred in a fall weeks earlier, and that Martinez provided a false confession. After Denver District Attorney John Walsh undertook his own investigation, he agreed to support the motion to dismiss the case against Martinez. But outside court, when a reporter asked him if this was a “wrongful conviction,” he did not specifically respond. “It was a case in which, at the end, the evidence that we had before us and the reassessment of the underlying medical records led us to believe that had … these challenges to the cause of death been presented at the time of trial, there might have been a different result,” Walsh said. “So, to that degree we agreed that this is a situation where the criminal justice system needs to take a look at how it works and correct itself if necessary.” Walsh’s spokesman, Matt Jablow, said Wednesday he could not discuss the question of whether Martinez meets the standard of “actual innocence.” Lawrence Pacheco, spokesman for Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser, said that office will represent the state once a compensation request is made and, as a result, no one from that office could discuss it. Robinson, the 9NEWS analyst, said the burden of proving actual innocence falls to Martinez. “A court or a jury has to determine that there really was a miscarriage of justice and that they had no role at all – entire innocence – as it relates to the crime in question,” Robinson said.
